# EPISTLE

...from where I have taken the beginning of my writing; you will understand. I, therefore, am entirely unknown to you, and you are indeed unknown to me in face; but in spirit—which is the true and inner man—you have recently become most well-known to me. For indeed, when three days ago <note>original: "nudius-tertius," a Latin idiom for "the day before yesterday" or "three days ago"</note> it happened that I was crossing over the bridge of the Rialto <term>Rivi alti: literally "Deep Stream," the Latin name for the Rialto district and bridge in Venice</term>, a certain small book was offered to me by a friend who is also known to you. It was a new publication <note>original: "nunc primo excusus," literally "now first struck," referring to the printing press</note>, marked on the back with the coat of arms of the current Pope, and containing your elegant letter addressed to that same Pope. Its title was *On the Ruin of Satan’s Tyranny* <note>original: "In Sathane ruinam tyrännidis"</note>. I soon purchased it <note>original: "ære redemptum," literally "redeemed with bronze," meaning bought with coin</note> and took it home with me to read more conveniently. And so, given the opportunity of leisure, I began to read; nor did I stop, owing to the delight I took in the desired subject matter, until I had tasted the whole work by reading it through. I read, therefore, your scholarly labors <term>lucubrationes: literally "works produced by candlelight," a term used to describe diligent, late-night intellectual effort</term>, from which I drew my knowledge of you; I read the holy vision-

<summary>Sylvester describes a chance encounter on Venice's Rialto Bridge where he purchased Paul Angelus's book, "On the Ruin of Satan’s Tyranny." He explains that reading this work made him feel as though he knew Angelus intimately despite never having met him in person.</summary>
<keywords>Rialto, Venice, book trade, Pope, Satan’s Tyranny, scholarly labors, intellectual friendship, inner man</keywords>

# DEDICATION

I did not shudder to undergo <note>original: "subire nō horrui," continuing the thought of accepting a difficult or divine task from the previous page</note>. You could not (you say) read anything else, for the holy man did not permit it; he who then showed you the **seven seals** <term>signacula septem: In the biblical Book of Revelation, these seals secure a scroll containing God's plan for the end of the world; opening them triggers a series of apocalyptic events.</term> of the whole book, of which four had already been set aside and already loosened, and the remaining three were yet to be loosened and opened.

One of these he held in his hands, and then, in your presence, a sacred and glorious **resounding trumpet** began to sound; he loosened one of the aforementioned seals, and perfectly opened the **fifth seal**. Looking around at this and trembling with fear, you fell upon your face, and upon the **altar of God** you saw the souls of countless slain people <note>original: "animas interfectorum," a reference to Revelation 6:9, where the souls of martyrs who died for their faith are seen under the altar</note>, and you heard many voices all around, crying out without end: "Woe, woe, woe!" <note>original: "veh, veh, veh," the traditional Latin cry of lamentation corresponding to the biblical "Woe to the inhabitants of the earth."</note>

You saw other greater and more extensive things following, which you claim you are unable to recount, even if a long space of time were granted to you. You recite these things and even more extensive ones in your **letters**. For that reason, [the scent] of your holy virtues...

...so that I may be made worthy of his grace. At **Venice**, in the **Island Monastery of Saint Christopher** <note>original: "Insulari Locello divi Christophori." This refers to San Cristoforo della Pace, a monastery on an island (now part of San Michele) in the Venetian lagoon.</note>, on the **Ides of June** <note>June 13th</note>, 1525.

*For a greater understanding of the mysteries contained in this and other small works by this author, one must first consider those things which the author himself places at the beginning of his exposition on **Isaiah**. Specifically, he first sets forth the **three states of the world** <note>Joachim’s "Three Ages" (Ages of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), which form the core of his prophetic history.</note>, beginning from **Adam** and proceeding until the end of time. Then, he describes certain concordances and agreements, or combinations, along with the significance and meanings of different times.*

*He also presents the **mystery of the church**, which revolves annually, depicted within the **dragon** <note>A symbolic representation where the history of the church is mapped onto the body of the dragon from the Book of Revelation.</note>, beginning from its head and from **Septuagesima** <term>Septuagesima: The third Sunday before Lent, traditionally marking the start of the pre-Lenten season in the liturgical calendar.</term>. Through this are declared and signified the tribulations and pressures which the church has suffered and is yet to suffer until the end of the world, as well as the consolations and divine aid.*

*He presents the time **before the Law**, the time **under the Law**, and the **time of Grace**, along with their **sacraments**: the **Trumpet**, its symbolic form and meaning; and the **Seals** and their openings <note>Refers to the opening of the seven seals in Revelation 5–8.</note>.*

*He presents a **dragon of another form**, having **seven heads**, which designate seven pressures or battles: namely, all the evils which the church and its members have suffered and will similarly suffer throughout seven periods of time.*

*He presents the **Psaltery of Ten Strings** <note>A reference to Joachim’s work "Psalterium decem chordarum," where he uses the ten-stringed harp as a mathematical and musical metaphor for the Holy Trinity.</note>, in which we are instructed how to flee from, conquer, and overcome the snares of the serpent and ancient enemy. This was prefigured in **David**,*

And it should be noted that under the seventh head, a certain confusing mixture of time will occur; so that in the future, the chaff of this world—being tossed more violently than usual along with the wheat—sometimes rest may smile upon the weary, and sometimes labor may be imposed upon those at rest. <note>An allegory for the tribulations of the faithful (the wheat) being tested alongside the wicked (the chaff) before the final judgment.</note>

But it must be known that the heads of the dragon are one thing, and the heads of the beast from the abyss—representing the surging of the unfaithful people—are another. This is because the heads of the dragon began with that Herod who persecuted Christ; but those of the beast began with Chosroes, who moved battle against the sons of the virginal Church. For although such pestilential men are members of the devil and pass into the single body of the Antichrist, the heads of the fourfold beast <note>Referencing the beast with four heads from Daniel 7 or the general apocalyptic beast.</note> are nonetheless to be referred to the cruelty of the Sultans within the Saracen sect, destined to proceed until those times when all the kingdoms of the world opposing the scepter of Christ will be crushed, as if in the feet of the Babylonian statue. <note>A reference to the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2, where a statue representing worldly empires is destroyed by a stone representing the Kingdom of God.</note> Indeed, the ten horns of the beast, in this sixth time, are to be united in some way to the crowd of unclean nations, so that they may both crush the beast by a just judgment and destroy the Muhammadan people from the earth.

## The Form of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery.

In this figure are shown the three groups of fifty Psalms, representing the three persons of the Godhead and the three ages of the world, symbolized by the one hundred and fifty fish <note>A reference to the miraculous catch of fish in John 21:11, often interpreted by medieval theologians as symbolizing the totality of the elect</note> mentioned in John 21.

<margin>Psalms:</margin>
<margin>Genesis 12.</margin>
Scripture teaches that the ten strings are mystical, encompassing all generations of the world from Abraham to the very last of the elect.

Therefore, the first horn of the psaltery is not pointed like the other two lower ones: because the Father, remaining at the peak of majesty, is never described as being sent, but only the Son and the Holy Spirit were sent into our narrow straits <note>A metaphor for the earthly realm or the limitations of human existence</note>.

Note that man is set above all the orders of angels because of the Word of the Father assuming human flesh: so that He might restore the tenth rank <note>In medieval theology, humanity was often seen as the "tenth rank" created to fill the void left by the fallen angels</note> of the string, which had fallen.

Moses wrote the <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments (from the Greek 'deka', ten, and 'logos', word)</term> of the Law (Exodus 34). Paul, however, wrote the word of the cross to ten Churches (1 Corinthians 1).

The first string begins from fear and ascends to the height of charity <term>charity: "caritas" in Latin, referring to the highest form of divine love</term>.

<margin>Luke 18.</margin>
<margin>John 14.</margin>
<margin>Titus 1.</margin>
Note that two are sent by one, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit by the Father; and one is sent by two, namely the same Spirit. Hence in the Creed <note>The Nicene Creed, a foundational statement of Christian belief</note>, it is said: "Who proceeds from the Father and the Son" <note>original: "Qui a Patre filioque procedit"</note>. The Greeks do not accept this <note>A reference to the 'Filioque' controversy, a major cause of the schism between the Western (Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) churches</note> because they do not understand, imitating that blind man who, standing by the road, cried out: "Lord, have mercy" <note>original: "Kyrieleison"</note>. For they do not walk in the way of truth, which is Christ, but wander beside it. "They profess," he says, "to know God, but by their actions they deny Him."

*South.* Where the face of the Eagle is found: **Allegorical Understanding**, which is engaged in three modes: the tropological <note>the moral or figurative application to the soul</note>, the contemplative, and the anagogical <note>the mystical sense relating to eternal life and the future glory of heaven</note>.

*North.* Where the face of the Man is found: **Moral Understanding**, which deals with the nature of vices and virtues.

*East.* Where the face of the Lion is found: **Typological Understanding**, which is divided into seven species, as if it were a river: like the river of Egypt <note>the Nile</note> divided into seven streams.

*West.* Where the face of the Ox is found: **Historical Understanding.** This form of understanding differs from the mere literal history <note>suggesting that "intelligentia historica" involves a deeper comprehension of the facts of the past than a simple reading of the events</note>.

# HERE BEGINS THE HYMN BY THE SAME
### Abbot Joachim <note>original: "Abbatis Ioachim"</note> concerning the heavenly homeland.

O happy kingdom, homeland on high: in which the ranks of saints find rest: all things decorated with great glory, in perennial peace.

It is not within the power of a writing pen to mark, nor for the tongue of an eloquent man to tell: how great are the things the eternal God has prepared for those who shall reign in you.

For you sighs the lost offspring of the human race, fallen through our first parent <note>referring to Adam</note>: but redeemed by the death of the Redeemer sent from heaven.

Well does the soul sigh, consigned to the darkness mentioned, which, deprived of the joys of paradise: has lost the light which the citizens on high enjoy forever.

For by the splendor of the present light <note>the temporary, earthly light</note> the blind crowd of youths is deceived: thinking that which fills the world is pleasant, though it leads to perennial weeping.

For what can a man who is destined to die do, except weep for his miserable ruins: and mourn during the brief time of his dwelling here?

Truly, he is very wretched and unhappy who, while he lives, does not realize he is an exile: who does not sigh for the happiness of that kingdom.

Oh, if anyone could taste the feasts of that kingdom in the palate of the heart: he would despise all the pleasant things that this present life falsely promises.

Yet it is no wonder if a work is noted as being deservedly distinct for the sake of the creature: prepared beforehand as a threefold structure for the good, the evil, and those in the middle.

For heaven, earth, and hell <note>original: "inferus"</note>, considered together, each demonstrate their own nature: while in respect to each, every single thing is weighed.

Hell is a place of darkness below: above is the heaven of eternal light: remaining in the middle is the dry land <note>the Earth</note> common to both.

Hell includes no angels: the kingdom on high <meta>catchword: spiritus</meta>

<margin>2 Thessalonians 2.</margin>
**Anagogically** <note>The "anagogical" sense interprets the text in light of its eternal or spiritual significance regarding the end of time.</note>, the watchful rod is the Holy Spirit, concerning which [it is said] "the rod of his mouth," that is, the spirit of Christ, shall slay the wicked one, that is, the devil.

<margin>Psalm 74.</margin>

Therefore, the <term>prelates</term><note>High-ranking members of the clergy, such as bishops or abbots.</note> are found in the iron pillar; the teachers in the bronze wall; and the subjects in the city. To the **Kings of Judah**, meaning the virtues of the soul flowing into the church prelates, the teachers of truth, and its leaders. All such people will wage war against the preachers who are to be revealed;

### ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH.

...and they should lead back their customs among unrefined and very bad clerics to the worship of justice, in all holiness.

Note the three types of water: **Drops**, **heavy showers**, and **rains**. **Drops** are the finer words <note>original: "subtiliora verba," referring to deep theological nuances or intricate explanations</note>; **rains** are warnings; **heavy showers** are rebukes. Accordingly, the first group of teachers are the **expositors** <note>those who explain the meaning of scripture</note>; the second are the **evangelizers**; and the third are the **pourers** <note>original: "effusores," those who pour out the spirit or intense correction</note>. They explain subtly, they evangelize sweetly, and they pour out strongly: subtly toward the righteous, sweetly toward the lazy, and strongly toward the hard-hearted.

Regarding the **late rain**, <note>original: "Serotinus," the final rain before harvest, used by Joachim to symbolize the final spiritual outpouring of history</note> he says that it is necessary in these days for God to bring forth **clouds** from the ends of the earth—that is, from all Christian peoples. 
<margin>Regarding the new preachers.</margin> 
These clouds, through the rain of spiritual preaching, produce the **lightning** of miracles and 
<margin>Luke 1.</margin> 
corrections. To provide knowledge to 
<margin>Jeremiah 10.</margin> 
his people—whom he will yet choose from "Israel," meaning the Christian people—he brings forth the **winds** of manifold understanding from the treasures of the scriptures. 

Note these three:
1. **Winds**: These are the expositors.
2. **Clouds**: These are the announcers.
3. **Lightning**: These are the correctors.

This is so that some may be like the **Cherubim**, others like **Angels**, and others like the **Seraphim**. They bring forth wisdom among the perfect; they suggest 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> 
repentance among the imperfect; and among the 
<margin>Psalm 119.</margin> 
wicked, they rightly scatter **"coals of desolation,"** <note>original: "carbones desolatorios," a biblical image for divine wrath or severe rebuke</note> which is to say, they spread righteous anger. 

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 31.</margin> 
He is praised who could have done evil and did not; he is 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 22.</margin> 
blamed who abandoned the good and committed evil. He who could have done both but did not advance toward better things is "stoned with the dung of cattle." <note>original: "Lapidatur de boui stercore," a reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:2, which compares a lethargic man to a piece of filth; here it implies the shame of failing to improve one's soul.</note> This "stoning with dung" is the preaching of the rebuke of sin and the gain of time for grace. 

In the days of **Josiah**, King of Judah, the Lord spoke to me—namely, at the time when the **exile** <note>original: "transmigratio," referring to the Babylonian Captivity</note> was imminent.

# THE PROPHET JEREMIAH.

...with deception <note>The text continues from the previous page's sentence: "...thinking temporal peace would last, they are led astray with deception."</note>, he will convert them. He will utterly lay waste to the "cities"—meaning the carnal senses, thoughts, and actions—and he will make them void of the beastly spirit <term>beastly spirit: a life led by animal instincts or carnal desires rather than reason or grace</term> that once inhabited them. And because those who were long dead in sins will now live according to reason, they will gird themselves to run the blameless path through obedience. Clothed in haircloth <note>original: *cilicio*; a rough garment worn as a sign of repentance</note> and living a harsh life, they will mourn with longing and howl over the eternal fire. 

But the hearts of the king, the princes, the priests, and the prophets—namely, all the clergy and the religious orders—will be stunned that men are being converted to penance in such a way. They themselves will tremble and perish—that is, they will fail <gloss>Latin: *deficient*</gloss>—by living and thinking perversely. Deceived by the peace of the world, which promises prosperity, they will instead follow the true peace, which brings the sword of God’s word all the way to the soul, separating it from the death of sin and the world, toward the life of the kingdom and the spirit. 

It follows: *A parching wind in the ways of the desert of the daughter of my people, not to winnow nor to cleanse.* <note>Jeremiah 4:11</note> The "desert" is the world, whose "ways" are wicked actions; in these, the "way" is the imitation of the daughter of my people—namely, the Church. The "wind" is persecution; "parching" means consuming, not winnowing or cleansing. Instead, it is confounding, involving everyone and discerning no one. *A full spirit from these shall come to me* <note>Jeremiah 4:12</note> because it will be fully afflicted. 

The "parching wind" is first like a lion, and secondly like a wind. A lion because of boldness and constancy of faith; a wind because of the lightness of poverty <note>In Joachimite thought, the "lightness of poverty" refers to the voluntary poverty of the new spiritual orders</note> and the subtlety of religion. It is "parching" because of the knowledge of preaching and the fire of charity. It is "in the ways"—that is, in the hearts—of the "desert"—that is, of the human race—in which is the way of the daughter, that is, the faithful. For regarding the souls committed to her, the "Way"—that is, the zeal—of the Church ought to be for the salvation...

### ABBOT JOACHIM ON [THE PROPHET JEREMIAH]

...the salvation of my people, whom I have redeemed with my blood. <note>original: *salutem populi mei, quos redemi in sanguine meo*</note>
<margin>Revelation 5</margin>
They do not come for the purpose of winnowing, as if to separate the sinner from the righteous like chaff from wheat, nor merely to cleanse by removing filth. Instead, they come just as Isaiah says: *The colts of the asses shall eat mixed fodder,* <note>original: *Pulli asinorum commixtum migina comedent*; likely referring to Isaiah 30:24. The "mixed fodder" represents the mixture of different types of people or teachings.</note> so that they might enclose both the good and the bad together in the "dragnet" of doctrine and religious life. From this mixture, a "full spirit"—that is, a spirit of contrition and praise—may emerge and ascend to God. God speaks His judgments with them through a penance that is to be emulated. Likewise: *Behold, he shall ascend like a cloud, and his chariot shall be like a storm.* <note>Jeremiah 4:13</note> The marvelous deeds of the doctors <term>doctors: in this context, the great teachers, theologians, and preachers of the Church</term> are recounted here, as they are described now as an ox, now as a wind, now as a cloud, and now as a chariot with horsemen. They run together: with the "lion" of the shepherds, with the "burning wind" of men, with the "cloud and storm" of the doctors, and with the "chariots and horses" swifter than the eagles of the virgins.
<margin>Lamentations 4</margin>
Of these it is said: *Whiter than snow toward the north; more shining than milk toward the east; ruddier than ivory toward the west; more beautiful than sapphire toward the south.* <note>original: *Candidiores niue... nitidiores lacte... rubicundiores ebore... sapphiro pulchriores*</note> Thus, they are "lions" regarding their faith in the Resurrection; they are a "burning wind" regarding their patience in the Passion <term>Passion: the suffering and death of Jesus</term>; they are "clouds" regarding the humility or the humanity of the Incarnation; and they are "chariots and horsemen" regarding the vision of the Ascension.
<margin>Ezekiel 1</margin>
Regarding these, Ezekiel says: *Behold, a whirlwind.* <note>Ezekiel 1:4</note> These are the preachers who "whirl" or throw everyone into turmoil, rendering them "disturbed" so that they no longer serve the anxieties of the world, but instead find rest in the service of God. For those who are thus "thrown into turmoil" or disturbed come to penance for their sins. They come from the "north"—that is, away from the malice of the world and the temptation of the devil. And there was a great cloud.

Note that the preachers began from the north, that is, from the prelates <term>prelates: high-ranking church officials, such as bishops or abbots, who hold authority</term> of the Church. This is because angels first appeared to the shepherds who were keeping watch in the "north" and in the night. 
<margin>Luke 1</margin> <note>The text cites Luke 1, though the account of the shepherds is found in Luke 2.</note> 
Second, they work through a whirlwind—meaning the troubled and afflicted subjects in this world, who are as if traveling on the paths of the desert. 
Third, they work through clouds—the masters and teachers of secular writings, and even, in a literal sense, of the divine scriptures. These men spoke great things, perhaps even with pride rather than the humility of charity which builds up; they spoke from the kind of knowledge that "puffs up." 
<margin>1 Corinthians 8; 1 Timothy 4</margin> 
Fourth, they work through an enfolding fire—meaning the members of religious orders <note>original: *religiosos*; referring specifically to monks or friars living under a rule</note> who enfold the freedom of the spirit within the service of active work, which is "useful for a little." 
<margin>4 Kings 2</margin> <note>Known as 2 Kings 2 in modern Bibles, describing Elijah's ascent to heaven.</note> 
For in the fourth place, Elijah ascended in a fiery chariot, with horses and a splendid belt surrounding them—representing the mantle of sevenfold grace. At this sight, the waters of the Jordan—representing the Christian people—were divided during the preaching of the apostles. These waters will still fail and cease their worldly course in the case of future preachers, so that the "ark" of the contemplative life <term>contemplative life: a lifestyle dedicated entirely to prayer, meditation, and the direct experience of God</term> may pass freely through those divisions. 

Now, the stones of the Jordan which were chosen and taken out 
<margin>Joshua 3</margin> 
were the preachers of the first age, namely the apostles who were sent to the nations. However, from those same nations others are still to be chosen—as if from Gilgal <note>original: *galgalis*; Gilgal was the first campsite of the Israelites after crossing the Jordan, often interpreted as a place of transformation</note>, which represents the whole Church—and sent to unbelieving Christians. They are to be established in the Jordan in the place of the others; just as the apostles were guided at the beginning of the "second state," so these preachers are to be directed at the dawn of the "third state." <note>This refers to Joachim of Fiore’s famous "Three Ages" of history: the Age of the Father (Old Testament), the Son (New Testament), and the Holy Spirit (a coming age of spiritual perfection).</note> This is so that Christians do not become forgetful of their own salvation, and so the promises of the Spirit of the Lord might be seen in some way even in the "dust" of the Lord’s word as spoken in the Gospel. But because in the Trinity of God, the Spirit of the Lord is one of the persons...

It is fitting that the whole world should know this: *just as the Father worked in the first <term>state: or "age" (Latin: status); Joachim's influential theory that history is divided into three overlapping eras corresponding to the Trinity</term>, and the Son in the second—concerning which it is said, "My Father works until now, and I also work" <note>original: "Pater meus vsque modo operatur, & ego modo operor"; quoting John 5:17</note>—so the Holy Spirit will work according to the proper nature of the mystery. One should neither be troubled nor doubt simply because full liberty has not yet been granted to the Christian people, nor rest given from the labor of the Church; for in truth, until the new things are born, it is necessary to use the old. 

For example: the first state was designated from the departure of Abraham <note>original: "Habrae"</note> from Chaldea until the crossing of the Red Sea by the children of Israel. The second state began from Moses fleeing into Midian <note>original: "Madian"</note> and from Aaron, continuing until the crossing of the Jordan. The third state began from the spies being sent into Canaan, until the time of the Judges. Thus it is clear that before one state had completely passed away, the next is seen to have succeeded the other. For in the first state, the persecution of the Egyptians remains; in the second, that of the Canaanites; in the third, that of the Philistines. 

Do you not see now that the first state of the world was born in the dispersion of the Jews under Titus <note>the Roman Emperor who destroyed the Second Temple in 70 AD</note>? The second state, the end of which we are now enduring, is to be finished under many kings who rise against a Christian people who have turned away and apostatized from the faith and work of Christ—having turned indeed into a "Babylon"—kings who will come from the rising of the sun to exterminate nations. The third state, whose beginnings from God are now obscured so that the freedom of the spirit shines only a little, will be ended under the persecution of Gog <note>a biblical figure representing the ultimate enemies of God's people in the end times</note>, whom [the Lord], coming to judgment...*

It follows: After the raven, a dove clothed in variety is sent forth. Note that the raven is black, loves carcasses, and has a loud voice. On the contrary, the dove is agile, varied, avoids carcasses, and has a moan instead of a song. In all things there is variety. Those preachers will be black with the sadness of the heart, not of the world; grave in their life, eloquent in doctrine, and kind through compassion for their neighbor. The dove is more fertile in offspring, varied in the feathers of the virtues, agile in obedience, and is nourished by the grain of the chosen—namely, the scriptures. In place of the song of preaching, it possesses lamentation for sins and a desire for the heavenly homeland. So too was John [the Baptist] "black" in his food, which was the locust <note>original: "locusta"; Joachim interprets John's asceticism through this "darkness" of the raven</note>; he was grave in his life, [telling] the brood of vipers to flee...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Jeremiah Chapter 7. The previous page discussed the temple of Rome and how internal faith is more important than physical structures. ON JEREMIAH THE PROPHET

<margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin>
...[tribu]lations aspire. They swear falsely who destroy faith with their works; they offer libations to Baal <term>Baal (Baalim): an ancient Canaanite deity, used here to represent the idol of greed</term> because they serve greed: and to foreign gods, that is, to all other vices. Or certainly they offer libations to Baal who worship the gold of prelates <term>prelate: a high-ranking church official</term>; and to foreign gods and other canons <term>canons: here referring to ecclesiastical rules or the officials who follow them</term>, in whose wicked works they agree. 

Shiloh and Ephraim signify the Church of the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, which God rejects in its malice and errors, and whose destruction is near. Judah represents the Church of the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>; both will be destroyed at roughly the same time because both have sinned against the Lord. Although the Eastern Church must be scourged first by the nations, one must not pray for such people; instead, one must rise up against them. 

"Do you not see what these people are doing? In the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, the children gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough <note>original: "adipem," literally fat or richness, but used in the Latin Vulgate to mean the dough or fatness of the cakes</note> to make cakes for the queen of heaven, and offer libations to foreign gods" <note>Jeremiah 7:17–18</note>.

This is happening today, namely, in the Western Church. The "cities of Judah" are the churches; the "streets" are the common people; and then there are the fathers, women, and children. In the "children," we see the clergy; in the "fathers," the prelates; in the "women," the laity. They gather "temporal wood" through greed; they kindle the "fire" of spiritual things through simony <term>simony: the buying or selling of church offices or spiritual privileges</term>; and they knead the "fat" of carnal relatives through worldly lust. <margin>Hebrews 10</margin>

<margin>Psalm 73</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 30</margin>
Hence: *Give me neither riches nor poverty, but only the necessities by which nature may be sustained in sobriety.* <note>Proverbs 30:8. In abundance, he grows decadent; in want, he murmurs. Yet this passage can be understood healthily as referring to those repenting in their hearts toward a greater perfection.

As if there were no prophet in Israel, the Lord complains as she wastes away in pressures and even in sins, saying: **Is there no resin, etc.**

## Chapter Nine.

<margin>Joel 2</margin>
**Who will give water to my head?** <note>Jeremiah 9:1</note> The **head** of the Church is Christ; the **water** is weeping. The **eyes** are the Apostles, from whom the Gospel fountain pours forth tears of compunction. Alternatively, the **head** represents the prelates of the clergy, and the **eyes** represent the teachers of the contemplatives. It is said to the first group (the prelates) that they should weep for the sins of those under their care and wash them with the water of doctrine by instructing them. To the second group (the teachers) it is given to groan more abundantly over the crushing of the wavering Church, both in the "night" of its adversity and the "day" of its peace. In the night: lest the Church, exhausted by labor, should succumb. In the day: lest, not being struck <note>original: "pulsata." Suggesting the need for spiritual discipline or the "knocking" of temptation even in peaceful times.</note>

<margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin>

I 42

The author notes three things: In the "land of the north" are the **lustful**; in the "great commotion" are the **proud**; and in the "voice of the report" are the **greedy**. Concerning the second: <margin>Matthew 2</margin> *“King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him,”* <note>Matthew 2:3</note> for fear that they might lose their kingdom and their cities. 

Concerning the third—namely the Simoniacs and <margin>Genesis 11</margin> <margin>The affliction and plundering of the Roman Church.</margin> the greedy—it is said that they wished to buy the grace of the Spirit, specifically from Peter <note>A reference to Simon Magus in Acts 8:18–20.</note>. 

Behold what kind of shepherds we have who are retreating from the "east" of faith! They build a tower of pride—a Babel of luxury—out of the bricks of greed. In the field of the world, Shinar <note>original: "Senar"; the plain where the Tower of Babel was built</note>, unfair sinners act like the stench of teeth <note>original: "fatoris dentium," possibly a reference to the "gnashing of teeth" or "fœtor" meaning stench</note>; the stench is sin. The lord is unjust, tearing and biting his neighbor. Using the bitumen <note>a tar-like substance used as mortar</note> of kinship instead of the cement of charity; and instead of the stones of virtue, they use bricks—that is, wealth—baked and refined by fire.

"A voice of a report, behold, it comes from the land of the north," <margin>N.B.</margin> namely from the reprobates and the **Germans** <note>original: "Alemanis"</note>. There is a great affliction and commotion of treacherous nations, so that he may make the cities—the churches of Judah and of the Roman See—into a wilderness. <margin>John 3</margin> <margin>Revelation 3</margin> <margin>Philippians 2</margin> That is, he makes them plundered, and "dwellings for dragons"—which is to say, for the malicious. 

Why? Because of three things: Because they have not heard the word of the Lord; because they are covetous; and because they seek their own interests and not those of God. Or certainly, the "cities of Judah" are the minds of those who confess God with their mouths but deny Him by their deeds. And for that reason, He renders them solitary and void of virtues, and turns their dwellings into...

<header>ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH. 143</header>
<sig>I 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: rally</meta>

...vices. But the devil-dragon is said to have seven heads, <margin>Titus 1</margin> of which it is said: <margin>Revelation 13</margin> <margin>Psalm 73</margin> *“You have crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters,”* <note>original: "Contriuisti capita draconum in aquis"; referring to Psalm 74:13 in modern Bibles (73 in the Vulgate).</note> namely, the heads of the princes among the baptized. The first head was in the time of the **apostles**; the second, in the **martyrs**; <margin>Matthew 2</margin> the third, in the **doctors** <note>the Great Teachers or Church Fathers</note>; the fourth, in the **virgins**; the fifth, in the **clerics and monastics**; the sixth, in the **crusaders** <note>original: "cruce signatis," meaning those signed with the cross</note> and the **faithful**; the seventh, in the **two future witnesses** <note>referring to Enoch and Elijah, who are expected to return in the end times according to Revelation 11</note>.

The first head of the devil was **Herod**, through whom—because he could not destroy Christ—he devoured the innocent children. The second was **Nero**; the third, **Constantine** <note>Constantine’s inclusion as a "head of the dragon" is unusual; Joachim may be referring to the Arian controversy or the worldly entanglement of the Church that began in this era</note>; the fourth, **Chosroes**, King of the Persians; the fifth, **Henry I**, prince of the Germans; the sixth, **Saladin**; the seventh, the **Antichrist**, King of the Patarenes <note>a name often applied to Cathar heretics in northern Italy</note>. Note: each figure is understood along with his successors. 

Observe the falling away. On the **first day** of creation, there were light and darkness: the apostles and the Jews. On the **second day**, the firmament in the waters: the martyrs among the idolaters and <margin>Genesis 1</margin> philosophers. On the **third day**, the earth germinating: the doctors, once the waters of the heretics were removed. On the **fourth day**, the luminaries: the virgins against the followers of **Muhammad**, so that they might shine upon the earth. On the **fifth day**, the fish, etc.: against the lustful, giving them an example of virginity. On the **sixth day**, man against the beasts: namely, the faithful against the **Saracens**. On the **seventh day**, the preachers of truth <margin>Revelation 10</margin> against false Christians. The monastics were bought from the earth, the laity from Egypt, and the clerics from the "iron furnace." Likewise, the land of Egypt is called hell, as it is a land of darkness; it is "iron" because it is cruel, and a "furnace" because it cannot be extinguished. It is cruel toward bodies and inextinguishable toward hearts. There, bodies will be like iron, the mercy of the soul like the nature of fire; the nourishment...

Joachim uses them as a symbol for the institutional church hierarchy.</note>, that is to say, over the greater prelates of the Cistercians <term>Cistercienses: a reformist monastic order to which Joachim originally belonged; he often critiques them for becoming too wealthy or politically involved</term>: the year of their visitation, which is to say, of the tribulation sent upon them. In the youths, the future preachers can be understood; the "sons" are their followers, that is, those of another subsequent order <note>Joachim frequently predicted the rise of new, more spiritual monastic orders</note>; the "daughters" are adversaries according to the literal sense, or perhaps the religious remnants of the penitent laity.

...neglects, the rain does not descend. *The earth*, he says, *has mourned and languished*; <margin>Isaiah 33</margin> it languishes in faith and mourns in its works. In the work of virtue and in the faith of encouragement. Therefore, the **earth** refers to the laity; the **grass of the region** refers to the clergy. The **beasts** <note>original: "anima"; likely a transcription error for "animalia" (animals/beasts) based on the context of Jeremiah 12:4</note> are the regulars <term>regulares: monks or others living under a rule, such as the Cistercians</term>, and the **birds** are the spiritual men. These are the ones saying: *He shall not see our end*—that is, the desolation of temporal things and the death of souls.

But the answer is given: *If you have labored running with footmen, how can you contend with horses? And since you were not secure in a land of peace, what will you do in the pride of the Jordan?* <note>Jeremiah 12:5. This verse is traditionally interpreted as a warning: if you cannot handle small trials, how will you handle the great ones to come?</note> This passage seems complex, even if it appears simple in the literal sense. The **footmen**, the **horses**, the **land of peace**, and the **pride of the Jordan** <note>original: "superbia Iordanis"; a biblical idiom referring to the thick, dangerous jungle or rising floods along the riverbanks</note> suggest a twofold interpretation. Thus, the "land of peace" is associated with the footmen, and the "pride of the Jordan" with the horses.

The **footmen** are the humble laity; the **horses** are the soldiers and proud tyrants. The first are like a "land of peace," while the second are like the "pride of the Jordan." Therefore, according to the first understanding: if you were not safe among the laity, you will be even less so among the clergy. In the second understanding: if you were not safe among the secular clergy, you will be even less so among the religious orders. Likewise, if you were not safe among the faithful, you will be even less so among the infidels. It is as if to say: if it is not safe for you among the peaceful, how much more dangerous is it among the discordant?

The **pride of the Jordan** is the Roman Empire; the **land of peace** is the Roman Church. If, therefore, your own churchmen oppress you, you will be oppressed much more forcefully by the secular powers. Indeed, this speech is directed against the prophet just as it was against Christ: whom his own people betrayed, and whom strangers killed. So too now, the Cistercians and the secular bishops have betrayed the doctrine of truth unto death. <margin>Matthew 26, 27</margin> And would that no more of the Christian people be cut off, only to be driven toward the outsiders. It has become

<margin>Song of Songs 1</margin> ...to me my inheritance, like a lion in the forest. <note>original: "mihi hæreditas mea, quasi leo in silua"; Jeremiah 12:8</note> From this: *The sons of my mother have fought against me.* <note>Song of Songs 1:5. Traditionally, this refers to internal strife within the family of faith.</note> *He who pursues his father is wicked and clings to evil.* The Gentiles may be understood as the **forest**; the Jews, joining with them as if they were lions, raged against Christ. But now it is also to be feared that the Christian sons—who were once the inheritance of God through faith—might join with the **Saracens** <term>Saraceni: a common medieval term for Muslims</term> and other infidels to persecute the Christian people who remain in the faith. *Is my inheritance to me a bird of many colors, or a bird dyed all over?* <note>Jeremiah 12:9. The "speckled bird" is a famous and difficult image in Jeremiah; Joachim interprets it as a symbol of mixed character or diverse groups.</note> Far be it! A Christian is a **bird dyed all over** in faith, but **discolored** in his works. A Jew was **dyed all over** in circumcision, but **discolored**—that is, mixed with the false accusations of foreigners (otherwise translated as "marriages with foreigners").

However, regarding the **discolored bird** and the **bird dyed all over**, I understand these as two orders: either the **Black monks** or the **White monks**. <term>Black and White monks: the Benedictines (who wore black) and the Cistercians (who wore white). Joachim often used these colors to symbolize different eras of the Church.</term> But it is better to direct this toward those future orders, designated by the **dove** and the **raven**, in whom the inheritance of God may remain, and of which it is said:

These represent the "head" of the mind, the "offspring" of good works, and the "wind" of pride <note>original: "elationis"</note>. The laity veil their minds by despising goodness; the clerics abandon their offspring by rejecting knowledge; the monks draw in the wind by fleeing discipline. If the married laity do not cultivate the earth, they fall into fornication; if the ordained clerics desert divine worship, they gape after rents and income; if the religious draw in the wind, they aspire to secular things.

### ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH ###

*...from their own rocks: as if they fail to attract others by the heights of their religion. There follows:* **Why**, *that is, for what cause; or certainly it is spoken in wonder or as a question.* <note>The author is commenting on Jeremiah 14:8.</note>

**Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay for the night? Why will you be like a wandering man, and like a strong man who cannot save?** <note>original: "Quare sicut colonus futurus es in terra... velut vir vagus & fortis qui non potest saluare"</note>

Note four things: First, the **settler**. Second, the **traveler**. Third, the **wanderer**. Fourth, the **weak one**. <note>The Latin *infirmum* usually means "weak," though the biblical text here uses *fortis* (strong) ironically—a man who should be strong but acts as if he cannot save.</note>

*The **settler** refers to preaching; the **traveler** to the Incarnation; the **wanderer** to the Resurrection; the **weak one** to the Passion. He came into the land as if into the synagogue of His own people; He turned aside into the Virgin* <note>Referring to the womb of Mary during the Incarnation</note>. *He wanders in the "stumbling block" of the Resurrection;* <margin>Alternatively: in reproach.</margin> *He is weakened in death.*

*But spiritual men are to be in the land of the Church in the manner of a **settler**, by cultivating the seeds of preaching; **travelers**, by living in poverty; **wanderers**, by running about in concern for others; and **strong ones**, by enduring tribulations. These are to remain with us for our help, so that we may be able to repel the enemy or adversary.*

**This people has loved to move their feet and has not rested, and they have not pleased the Lord.** <note>Quoting Jeremiah 14:10.</note>

*This refers to the people who are Christian in name, but not in deed. They loved to move their feet away from spiritual things; and they did not rest, that is, they did not cease from carnal things; and they did not please God—not so that He might rescue them, but rather punish them.*

...things. Concerning the first: **The just shall live forever.** <note>original: "Iusti in perpetuum vivent"; a reference to Wisdom 5:15.</note> Concerning the second: **The life of man upon earth is a warfare.** <note>original: "Militia est vita hominis super terram"; a reference to Job 7:1, suggesting earthly life is a constant struggle or service.</note> Concerning the third: **Who among you can dwell with the devouring fire?** <note>original: "Quis poterit habitare de vobis cum igne devorante"; a reference to Isaiah 33:14.</note>

Note three things in heaven, three on earth, and three in hell. In heaven: the sun, the moon, and the stars. In the world: misery, mud, and dregs. In hell: fire, snow, and the spirit of storms. 

The **sun** represents perfection; the **moon**, incorruption; the **star**, virtue and blessedness. **Misery** represents tribulation; **mud** represents ambition; and **dregs** represent corruption. **Fire** represents consumption; **snow** represents dissolution; and the **spirit of storms** represents a turbulent shaking.

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>

Regarding the first, namely heaven: God made two great lights and placed them in the firmament of heaven along with the stars. 

<margin>Psalms 10, 114.</margin>

Regarding the second, namely the world: **He led me out of the pit** <note>original: "Eduxit me de lacu"; referencing Psalm 40:2 (or 39:3 in the Vulgate). The text interprets the "pit" as the world.</note>—that is, out of the world—of misery, where there is affliction from the mud of greed and the dregs of lust. 

Regarding the third, namely hell: **Fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of storms.** <note>original: "Ignis grando nix glaties & spiritus procellarum"; referencing Psalm 148:8.</note> For this reason, snow alone is mentioned because hail and ice are types of snow. Truly, by the name of "snow," dissolution follows on both sides through hail and ice: by the **hail** of industrious punishment, and by the **ice** of shattering matter. 

Likewise, fire brings forth smoke where there is darkness. Clouds, driven by whirlwinds, bring hail and snow. The earth brings sulfur, the fuel for fire and stench. The wind and the cold of the north—that is, the devil and his darkness—bind the ice, both body and soul, so that they might not be dissolved in their punishments. It burns in such a way that it does not consume; it dissolves in such a way that it restores. 

This is the **other burning bush** which burns and is not consumed, from the midst of which Christ speaks to the human race, represented in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob...

The **sword**, so that the obstinate abstain from the Body of Christ. Regarding the **tomb**, so that they do not receive communion in the cemeteries with the faithful. Or certainly: famine in life, the sword in death, and casting out in punishment.

<margin>In the same place, chapter 8.</margin>
The sons [of God] desired the daughters of men, and there were giants: among the laity, these are famous men; among the clergy, they are the same. Likewise, famine represents greed: which, the more it afflicts one through loss, the more it grows through desire. This famine arises in Samaria—the church of the clergy—in which they trade in "dove's dung," meaning the revenues of the <term>regulars</term> <note>The "regular" clergy are those living under a religious Rule (regula), such as monks or canons. Joachim is criticizing the secular clergy for profiting from monastic resources.</note>, and the "donkey's head," meaning the offerings of the laity <note>original: "stercus columbarum... caput asini"; these are references to the extreme famine during the siege of Samaria in 2 Kings 6:25, where even waste and heads of unclean animals became expensive commodities. Joachim uses them here as symbols for corrupt financial transactions within the Church.</note>. Likewise, "Israel" represents the spiritual prophets: the teachers and priests of the Church, the abbots or priors. They have gone away into the "land," that is, into the lifestyle of the laity, through an unrecognized lust and through the greed of the clergy. They once despised such things when they stripped off their old life, yet they return to them for the exchange of personal gain.

<margin>Baruch 3.</margin>
To these it is said: *What is it, O Israel, that you are in the land of your enemies?* <note>Quoting Baruch 3:10.</note> It is as if he were saying: Even if the laity and the clergy overstep their bounds, those in the religious life should never have returned to the world through their own desires.

<margin>
Galatians 5.
Psalm 57.
Baruch 3.
Luke 16.
</margin>
The "land of enemies" is the life of the carnal laity who "lust against the spirit" <note>Referencing Galatians 5:17.</note>. The "foreign land" is the life of the clergy, who are alienated from the womb of true doctrine; they have wandered from the womb of a sober life and have spoken falsehoods through the wickedness of greed <note>Referencing Psalm 58:3 (Psalm 57 in the Vulgate numbering).</note>. Such a person is "counted among the dead," that is, among the lay sinners; he is with those who are in hell, like the rich man clothed in purple <note>The "Dives" of Luke 16:19.</note>. These are the clergy through the pride of their life: "clothed in purple" by their high rank; "in fine linen" by the outward appearance of righteousness; "feasting" through their gluttony; and "splendid" through their cupidity. Or, the "land" can mean this: some religious, even if they remain "dead to the world"—that is, ascetic—nevertheless remain in a kind of hell because of their weariness with life <note>original: "tedio vitae"; likely referring to 'acedia' or spiritual sloth, a common affliction in monastic life.</note>.

<margin>Note Well.</margin>
The "land of enemies" can also be understood as the land of the cruel Germans <note>original: "Alemanorum"; referring to the Holy Roman Empire, with whom Joachim and the Papacy often had conflict.</note>; the "foreign land" as that of the Saracens; the region...

...of the dead, the Patarenes <note>The Patarenes were a medieval heretical group often associated with the Cathars; Joachim views them as agents of spiritual destruction.</note>, the inhabitants of hell, and Gog <note>original: "gog gentium immundarum"; Gog is a biblical figure representing the enemies of God's people, often appearing in apocalyptic prophecy.</note> of the unclean nations. They are neither able to rain <margin>Baruch 3.</margin> like clouds, nor can they pour out the showers of the heavens—the dew of understanding that proceeds from the literal text. The teachers are in the clouds; the contemplatives are in the heavens. The former provide the rain of preaching and exhortation in the literal sense. The latter provide the dew and showers of rebuke and terror in spiritual understanding. *The ox represents the martyrs; the man represents the doctors <note>or "teachers."</note>; the lion represents the pastors or apostles; the eagle represents the contemplatives or virgins. In such as these, God rains down by preaching; he pours out showers by terrifying; he infuses the dew of grace. "Sculpted images" <note>original: "sculptilia"</note> are carnal teachers or philosophical doctrines, in which there is no spirit of life, but only the outward appearance of holiness.*

"God," he says,*

*...having been given over to a depraved mind <note>original: "sensum reprobum"; a reference to the divine abandonment described in Romans 1:28.</note> and a surely carnal understanding, specifically to the Christian people. They devastate with their heart what they also preach with their mouth. To the sword of chastity; to the dog of preaching; to the bird of contemplation; to the beast of action and labor.* For the *sword slays lust; the dog mangles worldly <term>animal wisdom</term> <note>original: "animali prudentia"; referring to purely natural or sensory wisdom as opposed to spiritual wisdom.</note>; the bird devours toward spiritual understanding; the beast scatters the glory of worldlings against pride.* "I will give them over," he says, "into rage among all the kingdoms of the ear[th]"...

...or who will take pity on you? <margin>Matthew 27</margin> Behold, another Pilate <note>Joachim uses Pilate as an archetype for a future secular ruler who will persecute the faithful.</note> is to come for the impious nations; he will not have mercy because he is cruel and merciless: cruel in respect to punishment, and merciless in respect to guilt—for inflicting punishment and for refusing to remove guilt. *   The **land** is tribulation from the heretical synagogue, dragging souls down to hell.

...they have [a share] of the work, <note>The text likely completes a thought from the previous page regarding the "spiritual men" or "future orders" participating in God's work.</note> God will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor: that is, the church received in its faith. He cleanses it from outward vices and earthly substances or affections; he pre-cleanses the consciences of the elect from mortal sins. These he will gather like chosen grain into the assemblies and the region of the righteous; but the chaff—the sinners—he will take up with the fire of penance, with temporal distress, and with the eternal fire of Gehenna <note>original: "gehennæ"; a reference to the valley of Hinnom, used here as a term for eternal punishment or Hell.</note> in the unquenchable underworld. <margin>Matthew 3</margin> Unquenchable charity can also be understood through fire, because "many waters have not been able to extinguish charity." <margin>Song of Solomon 8</margin>

"In the gates of the land": that is, because he will show those who were scattered to be in the streets of the church. Or, the "gates of the land" are the businesses of the world in which the faithful, under whatever name, are scattered by the tossing of the winnowing fan. <term>Winnowing fan: A tool used to toss grain into the air so the wind blows away the lighter chaff, leaving the heavy grain behind.</term> For I think that in those "gates," those future religious orders are designated: they are to be opened to sinners and those willing to hear, but closed to the reprobate and those who despise being taught.

By the name of "land," he means the conscience or the church. The winnowing fan is the preaching with which they shall winnow: toward the south for the luxurious; toward the north for the proud; toward the east for the merchants; and toward the west for the downtrodden. They repress the four winds of the world as if of the earth, so that they may not dare to blow upon penitent men. Thus, the south wind shall not truly behave wantonly; the north wind shall not lift one up; the east wind shall not enrich; and the west wind shall not cause despair. Let no one despair in guilt; let no one be enriched in vainglory; let no one be raised up in pride; and let no one behave wantonly in the petulance of the flesh.

<margin>Daniel 7</margin> Against these [earthly winds] are brought the four winds of heaven—that is, the heavenly virtues fighting against the world in the "great sea," which signifies the heart, when a great contrition of penance is sent by God. For against luxury is set chastity; against pride...

<summary>Abbot Joachim interprets the "winnowing" of Jeremiah as a spiritual purification of the Church, where preaching acts as a fan to separate the grain (the elect) from the chaff (sinners). <margin>Genesis 7</margin>

Mark this.*

The **fourth [age]** extends from David until the migration to Babylon: in which the Levites were ordained, and the worship of God was expanded. Some were appointed to lead the people; others to serve the tabernacle and the temple. The **fifth age** is from the migration to Babylon until Christ: in which some were cast away in Babylon, while others, having been granted liberty by Cyrus and Darius, ascended to the mountains of Jerusalem under the prophesying of Zerubbabel, Haggai, and Zechariah. And this is in exchange for the slavery in which the penitent serve the "gods of the earth" <note>original: "dijs terræ"; likely referring to the secular rulers or pagan influences the Israelites faced during the exile.</note> who are placed over them, and spiritual leaders, because the strong gods of the earth have been vehemently exalted.

The gall of bitter affliction is reserved, by which the blind and greedy man is enlightened; so too the liver of divine sweetness, by which the demon of carnal lust is put to flight from the holy animation <insert>otherwise: the removal or administration</insert> of the female sinner. For the first Egypt is the world. The second is the soul. The third is hell. 

In the first, there is palpable darkness. From this: *we have groped for darkness as if at noon.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 59:10 or Job 5:14, describing spiritual blindness in the midst of worldly light.</note> These are the three days of darkness among the Egyptians in speech, in knowledge, and in work; these were made over the earth when Christ was crucified.

# ABBAS JOACHIM ON JEREMIAH

<margin>Revelation 12.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 10.</margin>
...however, he is not a fisherman but a hunter. Hence: Nimrod <note>The Latin text uses the name "Neroth," a variant of Nimrod, the biblical figure often interpreted as the first tyrant.</note> was a powerful hunter and sturdy before the Lord. He was powerful in regard to oppressing; a hunter in regard to extorting; and sturdy in regard to scourging. He stood before the Lord thinking he was offering Him service: First, so that no one might shake off the yoke of his burden. Second, so that no one might break the scepter of his tax-collector. Third, so that the rod upon his shoulder would not be despised. The peasant is oppressed by labor; the servant is corrected by the rod of God; the citizen is plundered by taxation. The first is the burden of lust. The second is the rod of pride. The third is the scepter of greed. Concerning these, it is said 

<margin>Job 41.</margin>
that the devil has those who press themselves together with scales <note>Original: "squammis sese præmentes." This refers to the description of Leviathan in Job, where his scales are so tight no air can pass between them—symbolizing a community of sinners locked in their pride.</note>. What then shall become of these fish—these smooth ones <note>original: "imbricis"; possibly referring to a type of water creature without scales, or a typo for "imbeciles" (weak ones). Given the contrast with scales, it implies something unfit for consumption under Law.</note> without scales and fins? Let us cast them out so they do not occupy the waters uselessly; but let us place the good ones, who possess scales and fins, into the vessels of mercy.

### ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH.

<margin>Daniel 8.</margin>
...against the south of the Ethiopians. He does not say "against the west," because the male goat <note>original: "hircus caprarum." In Daniel 8, this goat represents the Greek Empire, but the author here reinterprets it.</note> of the Roman Empire raged from the west. From there, the male goat came from the west; his horns crush and scatter everything by trampling them down. Note that the goat did not touch the ground because of his pride—or perhaps because he crossed by sea. The "notable horn" represents the power of the Greeks. The eyes were two: Titus and Vespasian <note>Roman Emperors responsible for the siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note>. Eventually, as the empire grew against the horn of Greece, four horns rose up: the Arians, the Sabellians, the Eutychians, and the 
<margin>Daniel 7.</margin>
Macedonians <note>These were four major early Christian heresies that challenged the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity and the nature of Christ.</note>. The power of grace hamstrung their malice through the four winds of heaven, because from every side, against the power of the Greeks, the winds of heaven stirred up persecutors of the church. <meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on the Book of Jeremiah, likely by Abbot Joachim of Fiore. The previous page discussed the "curse" upon those who trust in man rather than God (Jeremiah 17:5). This page develops the imagery of the "tamarisk in the desert" compared to the "tree planted by the waters," using these botanical metaphors to describe the states of repentance, vice, and spiritual grace.</meta>

->## ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH.<-

For when someone, remaining under the curse of sin, thinks to advance by the flatteries and successes of the world: while he sees that the glory of the flesh is weighed down, the joy of the world slips away, and human life is shortened, by repenting of his faults he flees to the protections of the virtues. He hurries as if from the plains of Moab to the mountains of Judea <note>Moab often represents the worldly or carnal state in medieval exegesis, while Judea represents the spiritual or confessing state.</note>, and there he becomes like a **tamarisk** <term>mirica: a hardy, shrub-like tree (tamarisk) that grows in arid conditions; used here to symbolize a soul that has rejected worldly "fruit."</term> refusing to bear fruit in the world by rejecting worldly goods. Through this, he lives in the "dryness" of the spiritual life, and not in the "carnal fertility" of an uninhabitable land of salt. He posits three conditions: **saltiness**, **dryness**, and the **uninhabitable**.

Dryness is the absence of external vices; saltiness is the state of internal vices; "uninhabitable" refers to tribulations. In the first (dryness), there is no "rain" of carnal lust; in the second (saltiness), there is no "fountain" of human learning; in the third (the uninhabitable), there is no "sea" of diabolical temptation. The Jews identify the tamarisk as a *bruca* <term>brucas: though typically meaning a locust in Latin, Joachim follows a tradition identifying it here as a type of scrub or low plant</term>, while the Latins call it *broom* <term>genestras: the broom plant, known for its bitter taste and yellow flowers</term>, but both are infertile trees. Yet he calls both of these mature trees "bitter."
<margin>Jeremiah 14</margin>
Whether this refers to the reprobate or to those called to repentance, it is clear because both the wicked embitter the hearts of the gentle, and they embitter the minds of the perverse through justice in the present; otherwise, they are constrained in repentance rather than in eternal punishment.

**Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord: and the Lord shall be his confidence, and he shall be like a tree that is planted over the waters.** <note>Jeremiah 17:7–8. This is the positive counter-image to the tamarisk in the desert.</note> Just as those who live carnally in the desert of the world are understood by the name of the "tamarisk"—living in such a way that they never arrange to be healthfully uprooted from it—so the elect are called "a tree." These are the ones who flee from the dryness of the world to the abundance of the heavenly kingdom, having been uprooted from vices and transplanted over the flowing streams of virtue. Such people fix the roots of good thought toward the moisture of grace, and they do not fear the heat of carnal ten-

*The partridge has cherished what it did not give birth to; it gathered riches, but not with judgment. In the middle of its days, it shall leave them; and in its final end, it will be a fool.* <note>Jeremiah 17:11. **The Roman Church** is signified in the partridge. Having a zeal for God—but not according to knowledge—it cherishes the **Patarene** sect <term>Patarenes: a medieval dualist heretical group, similar to the Cathars. Joachim argues the Church "cherishes" them by failing to properly correct or convert them through true spiritual "birth."</term>, which it did not "give birth to" for cherishing, since it neither visited nor corrected them. Or perhaps it corrected them but did not "give birth," for it turns away from generating them in the true faith. It has amassed these "riches" <note>Referring here to the souls of the people or the influence of the sect.</note> thinking they were profitable to itself, or that its faith had been followed; but it was not with judgment, by which it might punish either the righteous or the unrighteous and separate the heretics from the faithful. 

And therefore, while the Church believed it should leave or punish that sect from nearby as it grew, nevertheless in the final end, when the persecution of the **Antichrist** is present, the Church will be a fool; for she will not be able to avoid his clever traps, which will subvert many of the learned and the faithful. 

Truly, if we look to the general course of the book: the "riches" are the believers whom you make into riches by not correcting their sins; nor did the Church give birth to them by grieving in their distress. The **partridge** represents the **prelates** <term>prelates: high-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</term>; if they had exercised judgment, God would not have left them in tribulation. And therefore they will be foolish, seeking earthly things, or perhaps they will be punish[ed]...

### JEREMIAH THE PROPHET
<page-num>257</page-num>

<margin>Romans 12. Philippians 4.</margin>
Against this, here: "The Lord led you into the land of **Carmel**: and having entered, you defiled it." <note>original: "Induxit vos dominus in terram carmeli," quoting Jeremiah 2:7. Carmel often symbolizes fruitfulness or the spiritual garden of the New Testament.</note>
<margin>Jerome</margin>
From the land of the Chaldeans—namely, the scripture of the **Old Testament** which was given to the Jews, who were of hard hearts—having gone outside (that is, from the servitude of the law), we have been led into the land of Carmel, the scripture of the **New Testament**. The knowledge of this scripture renders us circumcised from the vices of the body and the heart. Having entered into it through faith, we defile its <term>spiritual understanding</term> <note>The "spiritual sense" or "spiritual intelligence" (spiritualem intelligentiam) refers to looking beyond the literal words to find the hidden divine meaning.</note> either by interpreting it violently or by savoring it carnally. You see that we are drawn from the sterility of the letter into the abundance of the mystical spirit; yet, by wishing to live carnally, we defile it. Behold, we are led out of the world and led into the spiritual life; but by not living accordingly, we not only pollute that life but we "vomit it back"—that is, we reject it.

### [UPON] JEREMIAH THE PROPHET
<page-num>261</page-num>

...against it <note>This completes the word "contra" from the previous page's catchword.</note> on all sides by rising up. For that passage is ambiguous: whether it should be read as "in breaking apart" or "in plundering." 
<margin>2 Thessalonians 2</margin>

This is what the Apostle says: *He who now restrains, let him restrain, until he be taken out of the way* <note>original: "Qui tenet nunc teneat, donec de medio fiat." This refers to the "Katechon" or "Restrainer" mentioned in 2 Thessalonians 2:7, traditionally interpreted as the Roman Empire or the Papacy holding back the Antichrist.</note>, that is, he who now holds the empire: let him simultaneously hold the priesthood, and thus, wavering between both, let him be "taken out of the way," that is, let him perish, and be tossed about in the midst of the waves of the sea. 

<margin>Psalm 36</margin>

### ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH
<page-num>269</page-num>

<margin>Matthew 27.</margin>
...I think that man is the **Antichrist**, who through the leader of the **State** <note>original: "Reipublicæ"</note> will strip the clergy of their temporal <term>temporal: worldly or material assets, as opposed to spiritual ones</term> goods. Just as Christ was stripped of his garments by Herod and Pilate <margin>Ibidem <note>In the same place (referring to the Matthew 27 citation).</note></margin> <margin>Luke 23.</margin> so too the Church, sent naked onto the cross, shall be exposed to blows, insults, and scourges. He says **suddenly**, because of the urgency: for some will take the spoils as if they were members of the household; others will heap on insults as those who are hesitant; and others will inflict wounds like the unfaithful nations. The "members of the household" are the secular princes and soldiers; the "hesitant" are the heretics and their supporters; the "unfaithful" are the **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Muslims</note> and others coming from a treacherous land far away. All of these dig a pit in the earth of temporal things in order to trap the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops</note>, and they place snares of deception beneath their feet. Hence, **They have prepared a snare for my feet, and they have bowed down my soul.** <margin>Psalm 56.</margin>

<margin>Matthew 27, etc. Luke 23.</margin>
Note that Christ’s head is wrapped in thorns, his hands and feet are fixed with nails, and his side is pierced by a spear. The head of Christ—meaning the Christian people—are the **pontiffs** <note>Popes</note>; the hands are the **priests**; the feet are the other **faithful**, in whom it is necessary for Christ to be crucified again, resting upon them as if he were the Lord of the ladder of the universal church. Note these three things: the thorns, the nails, and the spear. The **thorns** are tribulations in temporal matters; the **nails** are <margin>Genesis 28.</margin> temptations in spiritual matters; and the **spear** represents oppressions in physical matters. Thus the distress of the church will be on every side, and she will not know what she ought to choose, because in the time of His fury God will cast them away—unless perhaps the thorns compress the **religious** <note>Those living under monastic vows, such as monks and friars</note>, the nails the **clergy**, and the spear the **laity**. For thorns tear, nails pierce, and the spear wounds. They tear by the sting, they pierce by the hammer, and the spear wounds by the shaft. By the sting of greed; by the hammer of **anathema** <note>original: "anathematis"; a formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note>—

### ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH

### Chapter 20

Pashhur <note>original: "Phassur"</note> the son of Immer <note>original: "Hemmer"</note> the priest, who was appointed chief in the house of the Lord, struck Jeremiah, and put him in the stocks <note>original: "neruum"; a wooden instrument of torture or confinement used to restrain prisoners</note>, which were in the upper gate of Benjamin in the house of the Lord.

*It is quite fitting that cardinals and even the supreme pontiff <note>the Pope</note> should strike those they deem "lying preachers" of the truth by afflicting them; they put them in the "stocks" by imposing silence upon them, so that they do not announce to the clergy the future evils coming from the Roman Empire. In the "upper gate of Benjamin" (it says), which signifies the strict Rule of the monks; or perhaps because in one of those orders many will be silenced, for they may be physically imprisoned due to the urgency of the coming tribulation. As for Jeremiah being released in the morning and naming the "terror on every side" <note>In the biblical text, Jeremiah renames Pashhur "Magor-Missabib," meaning "Terror on Every Side"</note> for the priests, this should not be understood as the prophets themselves fearing punishment. Rather, it means the prophets will strike terror into the hearts of the clergy and prelates—a terror to be brought upon them by the state <note>original: "republica"</note>. Hence Pashhur and his followers fell by the sword, and the house of Judah was given over to the governor of Babylon.*

<margin>Note well</margin>
*Let the Church hear that she is to be handed over into the hands of the Empire, both in her priests and her subjects; the sword of persecution will afflict them, stripping away the wealth, the labors, and the treasures of the high priests <note>original: "pontificum"</note>. First, the Empire will plunder; second, it will take everything away; third, it will lead them into Babylon—that is to say, shamelessly. It will plunder violently; it will take away through fraud; it will lead them confidently into Babylon <note>Babylon represents the state of captivity or the worldly power of the Antichrist</note>.*

<margin>Moral interpretation</margin>
*Moral interpretation:* The word of preaching is directed toward penitent souls, whom the heat of contrition so affects and consumes that they utterly fail while living in the fleshly body; this is so that the "bones" of virtues and strong deeds may sprout from the "clay" of the body, being set on fire by the fire of heavenly desire and charity. Hence: *The zeal of your house has eaten me up.* <note>original: "Zelus domus tuæ comedit me." From Psalm 69:9.</note>
<margin>Psalm 68 <note>In the Vulgate numbering; modern Psalm 69.</note></margin>

As for what follows, *He has delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of the wicked,* this is taken specifically to refer to those prophets who are to be spiritually afflicted. *Cursed be the day in which I was born: let not the day in which my mother bore me be blessed. Let that man be as the cities which the Lord overthrew, and repented not.* <note>Jeremiah 20:14-16.</note> Note that the man is cursed, the male child is born, the father rejoices, and the man making the announcement is overthrown. The day and the man are cursed, the mother grieves, the father rejoices, the male arises, the man is confounded, the day is cursed, and the mother is tormented. *That day* is the future tribulation; the *mother* is the Roman Church, under which the wickedness of men will be so great that she must necessarily be cursed by the prophet in her delicate <margin>Otherwise: dedicated</margin> womb. The *male child* is the <term>Seraphic Order|The "Order of the Seraphim," a term Joachim of Fiore and his followers used to describe a future, highly spiritual order of monks who would renew the Church; later associated with the Franciscans.</term> about to arise in the Church...

### ABBAS JOACHIM ON JEREMIAH

...ished. <note>The Latin text begins mid-word, "cta," likely completing a word such as "conducted" or "produced" from the previous page.</note> Thus Egypt is pressed on all sides: yet the Israelites, though immune from the plagues, are not immune from the labors of servitude. Therefore the prophet sees, grieves, and is troubled by the exit from the womb, and by the people passing over into vices or the harsh misery of the world. For this reason, the day of that one's tribulation—which is to say, our own—the day of the one who is raised up in prosperity, is called "evil." But the messenger is not exempt from it either, who, in order to act manfully against adversaries, persuades the Christian people toward the good. How many men are there today who approach the Supreme Pontiff as <term>couriers</term> <note>original: "equi cuniberes," likely a corruption of "equicibares," meaning messengers or riders.</note> and legates, persuading him to have the sign and the cross placed upon Christian shoulders? They do this so that while the intention is directed toward rescuing that reprobate and overturned Jerusalem, profit and temporal gain are wrung out from a show of piety. They do not consider how wicked it is to oppose divine counsels, especially where it concerns rebuilding the <term>foundations of Jericho</term> <note>According to Joshua 6:26, a curse was laid upon anyone who tried to rebuild Jericho. The author suggests that trying to rebuild the physical kingdom of Jerusalem is similarly cursed or contrary to God's current plan.</note> which are under a curse. Let the Supreme Pontiffs see and grieve for their own Jerusalem—that is, the universal Church not made by hands, which God redeemed with His own blood and not that of goats. Let them not grieve for that city which has fallen, and which causes others to fall over precious, muddy emptiness. Let them cease further to erect its walls, which daily collapse through the death of the faithful, shod—or rather, chastised—in its own feigned prosperity. For even if there is a struggle against the nations for the <term>Glorious Sepulcher</term> <note>The Tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem, the primary goal of the Crusades.</note>, the Lord is not going to translate that physical tomb into heaven; rather, He will translate the holy souls in whom the Lord is daily buried through the mystery of piety. In those souls He rests and remains, until He translates them and they rise again in the kingdom of eternal brightness.

**Typologically**: the **orphan** is the Christian people; the **prelates** are "Pilates" <note>Joachim uses a biting Latin wordplay here: "prælati sunt Pilati," suggesting the bishops are like Pontius Pilate rather than holy fathers.</note>, not fathers, but thieves and evening wolves; the **widow** is the Church, because they [the clergy] are not husbands but adulterers.
